rule_fidelity_rationale: rules[consequence]: The simulation faithfully shows mild performance costs from staying purely on internal tools and no severe sanctions or special rewards around spending, but because the assistant never actually authorizes a purchase, the positive-consequence pathway for justified purchases is not directly instantiated, so fidelity is slightly less than maximal.
rendering_fidelity_rationale: update-freq: Context, resources, and most actor updates follow the specified frequencies well, but peer purchasing behavior includes only one clear instance of an actual purchase plus several mentions of holding off, whereas the rule specifies peers should make or accept purchases in around three or four rounds, so purchase frequency is slightly under-instantiated.

overall_validity.rationale: Core variables (manager attitude, cost emphasis, authority scope, budget level, procurement strictness, deadline urgency, and peer norms) are instantiated very faithfully in roles, rules, and observed interactions. World updates for context, resources, and actors closely follow the specified patterns; the assistant’s central coordination role and moderate purchase authority are consistently reinforced. Consequence rules are mostly respected—manual-effort and coordination frictions appear when the assistant continues with internal tools, and there are no harsh overspend penalties or exaggerated praise for frugality—but because the assistant never actually executes a purchase within its authority, the positive-feedback branch for well-justified spending is not directly exercised. Rendering instructions are followed carefully, with immersive, event-based updates and no meta-commentary; the only notable shortcoming is that peers make actual purchases less frequently than specified, even though they do frequently consider and discuss them. These issues are minor and do not meaningfully contaminate the interpretation of the behavior under this configuration, so the simulation remains highly valid overall.
